title: Images and Misinformation in Political Groups: Evidence from WhatsApp in India
screen_reason: Reports quantitative shares of images circulating in public political WhatsApp groups in India that professional fact-checking journalists labelled misinformation, with explicit denominators (image shares and unique image clusters) and standard errors. This is the paper's stated purpose ('How prevalent is image-based misinformation on WhatsApp?'). The machine-learning half of the paper is detection work, which the protocol excludes, but the prevalence half stands on its own.

estimates.measure_type: % of image shares in public political WhatsApp groups that are misinformation (obvious misinformation plus previously fact-checked misinformation combined)
estimates.denominator: All image shares in the monitored corpus of 5,000+ public political WhatsApp groups in India (1.6 million images, 5 million messages, 250,000 users); estimated from 2,500 annotated images by inverse probability weighting with post-stratification on percentiles of number of times shared
estimates.definition: Image labelled by a majority of three professional journalists as 'obvious misinformation' or 'already fact checked to be false'; images on which the journalists obviously disagreed were dropped before analysis.
estimates.misinfo_def: "We asked the annotators to select from four options: 1. Obviously not misinformation 2. Obvious misinformation 3. Already fact checked to be false 4. Needs concrete fact checking." - no substantive definition of misinformation is given beyond the annotators' judgement plus fact-check-site verdicts.
estimates.n: 2,500 annotated images (500 random + 2,000 most-shared), weighted to 1.6 million images
estimates.source_quote: Clearly, misinformation makes up a substantial portion (13%) of all image sharing in these political groups, even if we are unable to conclusively label many images as misinformation or not.
estimates.page_loc: Findings, Finding 1 (p. 3-4); repeated in the Abstract, the Essay summary and the Implications section
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three independent professional journalists, described as 'experts in fact checking' who 'regularly report on digital platforms', annotated 2,500 images in a purpose-built portal that showed the image in its chat context and offered Google reverse image search against popular Indian fact-checking sites (altnews.com, boomlive.in, smhoaxslayer.com). Fleiss' kappa 0.42 over three classes (misinformation / not / needs concrete fact checking) and 0.78 over the two-class misinformation/not distinction; images with obvious disagreement were discarded, leaving 605 images labelled false. A further ~200 images were matched to ~20,000 images scraped from fact-checking websites using Facebook PDQ perceptual hashing.
estimates.moderator_quote: We obtained groups related to politics in India by manually searching for keywords related to all major national & regional political parties and religious groups and their prominent political leaders, looking for data on Facebook, Twitter and Google.
estimates.notes: The paper's headline number, stated verbatim three times ('making up 13% of all images shared on these groups'; 'We estimate that approximately 13% of image shares in our dataset are misinformation'; and the sentence quoted here). It is the authors' own rounded sum of their 10% 'obvious misinformation' and 3% 'previously fact-checked' figures and does not reproduce exactly from Table 1, where the shares column gives 11.1 + 3.2 = 14.3 and the clusters column 9.3 + 2.6 = 11.9; the prose paragraph is about clusters but says 'image shares'. Kept because the value is stated verbatim (R8 forbids the extractor computing sums, not the authors reporting one), but confidence is medium for that reason and rows 1 and 2 give the exact Table 1 cells. Construct: the corpus is images shared in group chats, so under the governing rule '% of shared items that are misinfo' this is SHARING/content_share, not CONTENT. ground_truth coded fact_checker because the coders are professional fact-checking journalists working against fact-check sites; an adjudicator who reserves fact_checker for published fact-check verdicts would code researcher_coding.

estimates.notes: Same coding as row 1 but a different denominator basis: distinct images rather than image shares, i.e. every image counted once regardless of how often it circulated. Flagged definition_variant=true so it is not pooled alongside rows 0-1. Judgement call worth an adjudicator's eye: a deduplicated set of distinct images could be read as 'all items that exist' and hence CONTENT, but every image in this corpus is a message someone shared in a group, so the paper's whole denominator is shares and all three rows are coded SHARING/content_share for internal consistency.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The 'Fact checked misinfo' Table 1 estimates - 3.2 (0.7) for shares and 2.6 (0.9) for clusters - are a subset of the same coding scheme and are the 3% component of the 13% headline; not given their own rows to avoid triple-counting the same corpus, but easily recovered from the same table cell if an adjudicator wants them. (2) The two raw sample proportions in Table 1 are sample statistics, not population estimates: popular 18.8 (0.9) misinfo and 7.0 (0.6) fact-checked among the 2,000 most-shared images (a rank-truncated, deliberately oversampled set, denom_selection would be curated), and random 10.7 (1.4) and 2.6 (0.7) among the 500 randomly sampled images. The IPW rows extracted here supersede both. (3) The 'Unclear' category is very large - 42.2% of shares, 41.8% of clusters, 43.3% of the random sample - so all misinformation shares here are lower bounds; the authors say so ('even if we are unable to conclusively label many images as misinformation or not'). This matters more here than in most included studies and should probably be flagged in any sensitivity analysis. (4) The typology shares - out-of-context images 'roughly 34% of our misinformation image dataset', memes 30%, photoshopped 'roughly 10%', top three categories 'over 70%' - are the composition of the misinformation set, not falsity shares within it, so they are not within_misinfo_content rows either. (5) Classifier accuracies (0.65-0.95) are detection performance, excluded by protocol. (6) Corpus composition (41% text, 35% images, 17% video; 24.4% of groups BJP-affiliated, 5% Congress) is not a misinformation share. (7) Annotation covered only 0.1% of images, and the group sample is acknowledged as non-representative ('the results from our analysis (e.g. prevalence of misinformation images) are only applicable to this dataset and may not generalize to the broader WhatsApp population') - a strong external-validity caveat for a number that gets cited as 'WhatsApp prevalence'. (8) Date: collection ran October 2018 to June 2019; year coded 2019 as the representative point (the 2019 Indian national election period the paper is built around).

rob.design: Non-probability frame of over 5,000 public WhatsApp groups discussing Indian politics, assembled by manually searching party, religious-group and leader keywords on group-directory websites, Facebook, Twitter and Google, then manually screened for political relevance; all messages in those groups collected October 2018 - June 2019 (5 million messages, 250,000+ users, 1.6 million images). 2,500 images (500 random + 2,000 most-shared) annotated by three professional fact-checking journalists in a purpose-built portal with chat context and reverse image search; four-option scheme; Fleiss' kappa 0.42 (three classes) and 0.78 (misinformation vs not); obvious-disagreement images discarded, leaving 605 labelled false; ~200 further images matched to ~20,000 scraped fact-check images via Facebook PDQ hashing. Prevalence estimated by inverse probability weighting with post-stratification on share-count percentiles, standard errors reported. Acknowledged biases: only public groups (fringe content in private groups missed), 24.4% BJP-affiliated versus 5% Congress, results explicitly said not to generalize beyond the dataset. Ethics approved by MIT COUHES with waiver of informed consent.
rob.item6_quote: We asked the annotators to select from four options: 1. Obviously not misinformation 2. Obvious misinformation 3. Already fact checked to be false 4. Needs concrete fact checking.
rob.item10_quote: We find that approximately 10% of image shares are obviously (to journalists) misinformation, with 3% more being misinformation that has been previously fact-checked.
